comments.author: hendrikmakait
comments.body: Note: The current implementation may cross the limit in some instances, i.e., any time we are starting to gather from a new worker. I'm working on some cleaner logic that avoids crossing the limit unless we are not gathering _any_ data. This change may also be moved to a separate PR if we want to get this general change merged.

comments.author: hendrikmakait
comments.body:
> Note: The current implementation may cross the limit in some instances, i.e., any time we are starting to gather from a new worker. I'm working on some cleaner logic that avoids crossing the limit unless we are not gathering any data. This change may also be moved to a separate PR if we want to get this general change merged.

I adjusted the logic and now we should never exceed the limit unless for the first task to gather to ensure that we make progress.

review_comments.author: hendrikmakait
review_comments.body:
> Why did we never see this?

So far, we only limited based on the # of connections. If you reached this point, you were guaranteed to have an additional connection available and we would always select as many tasks as possible to fill the message up to the limit. Now, we also limit based on the size of incoming data transfers. Thus, we might have a connection available, but the first task we'd try to gather for said connection would push us over the limit and `_select_keys_for_gather` returns an empty result.

> Shouldn't this be a continue?

No, at this point have reached the limit of what we should gather and break out of this loop.

review_comments.author: hendrikmakait
review_comments.body: Fair point, this makes an effort to hide unnecessary details and limit the assertions to what's important.

review_comments.author: hendrikmakait
review_comments.body:
> No, at this point have reached the limit of what we should gather and break out of this loop.

We _could_ `continue` and loop over all remaining workers in the hopes of finding another top-priority task that still fitis within the limit, but assuming roughly equal-sized tasks, the chances are slim that we will find one. We'd leave a bit of possible data size on the table, but my guess is that this doesn't really matter given the fact that we pulled the default out of thin air. There's much more to gain from optimizing the default than from tweaking the algorithm. So I'd rather stick with the early stopping variant and avoid looping over all remaining workers.
